limitations: Single engine-assisted reviewer used ordinary root and played replies before assessing outputs. Uncertain labels are retained. One position per source game.

cases.rationale: Qxg5+ forces Qg7 in the leading line and secures equality. The quieter queen moves let Black use the d-file immediately.
Qb1+ or Qe1+ gets checking tempo against the king to contain the e5 pawn. A quiet a6 allows Qxb6 and a materially different defence.
Black's rook and queen placements sustain kingside pawn pressure. The rook check leads to a trade, but the better queen move keeps more possibilities and the tactical distinction is unclear.
Rg2+ moves the exposed rook with tempo before Nd8. Nd8 first lets White capture the rook, and protecting the d-file and the active rooks matters in the continuation.
Rxg7+ forces the Black king out and enables the next rook check and Nxd7+. Queen exchange or a rook retreat loses the concrete attack.
Bd5+ forces a queen interposition and the follow-up exchanges win the rook on c8. The other bishop moves produce materially different lines.
g5+ wins space and improves the bishop and king position against the knight. The displayed alternatives differ chiefly in pawn structure and king access.
Re7+ gives the tempo to take the rook on h7. The passive rook moves leave Black able to coordinate the rook pair around the f-pawn.
The queen checks displace the king while preserving Black's passer. Qb1 and c2 remain a threat, and Nxg6 depends on exact checking order.
Bxe3+ trades the bishop and lets Black use the a-file without allowing the same rook checks. The alternatives offer materially comparable counterplay, with a specific forcing mechanism unclear.
Rxe2+ forces the king to h3 in the leading reply and Rh2+ diverts it before Qxf1. The other choices retain different forcing attacks.
Kg3 and Bb2+ coordinate the bishop, rook and king against the same pawn structure. The similar scores and differing replies give insufficient support for a decisive tactic.
